ety.text: From Middle English gille, gylle (“gill”), of North Germanic origin, akin to Danish gælle, Swedish gäl, Norwegian gjelle, and further to Old Norse gjǫlnar (“lips”), which also may have had the meaning of "gills" (based on Old Danish fiskegæln (“gills”)). The Old Norse word has been suggested as deriving from Proto-Germanic *gelunō (“jaw”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel-, which would make it root-cognate to Ancient Greek χελύνη (khelúnē, “lip, jaw”), χεῖλος (kheîlos, “lip”). Displaced native Old English ċīe.
From Middle English gille, from Old French gille (“a wine measure”), from Medieval Latin gillo (“earthenware jar”).
From Middle English gille, from Old Norse gil.
Clipping of gillian, from the female name Gillian.

senses.d: A breathing organ of fish and other aquatic animals.
ex: Fishes […] perform their respiration under water by the gills.

senses.d: A gill slit or gill cover.
ex: Gill nets are designed to catch a fish by the gills.

senses.d: One of the radial folds on the underside of the cap of a mushroom, the surface of which bears the spore-producing organs.
The fleshy flap that hangs below the beak of a fowl; a wattle.
The flesh under or about the chin; a wattle.
ex: dropsy fills you to the gills

senses.d: One of the combs of closely ranged steel pins which divide the ribbons of flax fiber or wool into fewer parallel filaments.
To remove the gills from a fish as part of gutting and cleaning it.
ex: She gutted and gilled the fish, then scaled it.

senses.d: To catch (a fish) in a gillnet.
ex: In cases of very heavy catches the nets may be hauled and stored with the fish still gilled. The fish would then be shaken out on return to the port.

senses.d: To be or become entangled in a gillnet.
ex: Since the fine threads of the net usually are caught under the gill covers of the fish they are said to be "gilled."
Also, when fish gilled there wasn't as much extra twine to tangle in, so they were easier to release from the net.

senses.d: A drink measure for spirits and wine, a quarter of an imperial pint or near to that amount, but varying regionally.
A unit of measure equal to 4 US fluid ounces (half a cup, a quarter of a US pint), approximately 118 milliliters.
A measuring jug holding a quarter or half a pint.
A rivulet, small stream.
A ravine.
A two-wheeled frame for transporting timber.
A promiscuous woman; harlot, wanton.
A prostitute.
ex: Gill comes from the Knight, that did so seek / To gaine her love; she's hir'd for a week.

senses.d: gill-over-the-ground: ground ivy.
gill-ale: an ale made with ground ivy among its ingredients.
To act as a prostitute.
ex: Comme proprement le fine of my Designs dey make; / Dam gilling Whore / Et Louis d'or

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin lāmella (“small, thin plate”), the diminutive of lāmina (“thin plate, knife blade”). This is the etymon of French omelette, English omelet.
From Latin lāmella (“small, thin plate of metal”).
